localChanges: The wave published cleanly (civ1-city 0.1.2, civ1-city-improvement 0.1.3, core-data-object 0.1.14, all verified against the registry and the pushed tags). Reinstalling the renderer against it exposed two tree problems, both of which had been quietly true for several stages.

`civ duplicates` finds any @civ-clone package with more than one live copy, by store entry rather than by version — the duplicated copies are often the *same* version, which is what made this invisible. Two copies are two modules, so a class from one is never `instanceof` the same class from the other, and nothing reports it. `civ publish` now runs it first and refuses on a hit, since `resolutionOf` reads that tree to decide npm-versus-git-push.

`civ stale` compares each installed copy against its checkout. This one found a false claim of mine: the committed lockfile pinned `core-turn-based-game@0.1.6` and `civ1-player@0.1.1` — the commits immediately before each `registerEvents` change — so every suite run cited as Stage 3 evidence used pre-change copies of exactly the two packages that stage's second half touched. With them installed the checksums are still 7d6b6b04 / 73a0cc05 / 3431063b and isolation is 13/13, so the change is behaviour-preserving; it is now measured rather than assumed. It defaults to every checkout, not the manifest, which records work *remaining* and lists 18 of 84.

The cause of both was this document's own post-wave step, `pnpm update '@civ-clone/*'`. A partial update re-resolves only what it names, and each publish of a GitHub-resolved package changes its tarball hash, so the renderer had accumulated three `civ1-city` tarballs, one per stage that published it. Replaced with a full re-resolve.

Also recorded: `npm publish` can return 202 Accepted with "being processed", so the registry 404s the new version for a minute. That is a third state beyond the two the gate knows, and `release()` pipes npm's stdio — read ~/.npm/_logs, not the wave log.

log: These tests constructed some registries and passed them to the rule factories positionally, leaving `playerWorldRegistry` and `workedTileRegistry` to default to the module singletons — which are shared with every other test file in the process. So the suite failed with "Wrong number of player worlds exist for player" depending on what had run before it.

The registries are now local and passed through, with `undefined` for the positional slots these tests do not care about. The part that is not mechanical is the state: `captured` looks up a `PlayerWorld` for the capturing player and previously found one only because another file had leaked it into the singleton, so each test now registers its own.
All three tests in this file pass; the suite is down from 8 failures to 5.
The remaining five, in `cost.test.ts` and `process-yield.test.ts`, need a decision rather than a pattern — see the note in the engine plan.

`base-city-yield-{population-support-food,unit-support-food, unit-support-production}` were declared as `github:` specs while `library-city` depends on them by range. pnpm honoured both, so the tree held two copies of each package — same 0.1.1 content, two module instances, two distinct classes.

`Rules/City/cost.ts` builds its yields from the npm copy; the tests compared them with `instanceof` against the copy re-exported through `../Yields`. Nothing matched, so `cost.test.ts` read `undefined` for PopulationSupportFood and UnitSupportFood, and reduced an empty array to 0 for UnitSupportProduction. `process-yield.test.ts` failed downstream of the same absent costs.

These three were the only `@civ-clone` packages duplicated in the tree, and the only ones the failing assertions named. Pointing them at `^0.1.0` like every other dependency leaves one copy and all 29 tests pass.

Also bind `captured.test.ts`'s `WorkedTileRegistry` to the test's own `RuleRegistry`. The no-argument constructor captures the singleton, where the fixture's `CanBeWorked` rule is not registered — and `[].every(...)` is `true`, so every tile reads as workable. It passes either way today; every sibling test already passes the registry.
Three separate defects, all of them the tests leaning on global state:

`created.test.ts` and `grow.test.ts` built every registry except `WorkedTileRegistry`, so `assignWorkers` wrote into the singleton and tripped over tiles another file had already claimed. Threading a local registry through `cityCreated`/`cityGrow` is not enough on its own: the no-argument `WorkedTileRegistry` constructor captures the *singleton* `RuleRegistry`, so `tileCanBeWorkedBy` found no `CanBeWorked` rule, and `[].every(...)` is `true` — every tile read as workable, including the ones already worked. Both suites failed in isolation for that reason, not from cross-file pollution. `new WorkedTileRegistry(ruleRegistry)` fixes it.

`build.test.ts` was flaky before any of this: civ1-science's `Player/added` rule hands each new player up to three random starting advances, and every `to.not.include` assertion in the file assumes a player who has discovered nothing. Which tests failed changed run to run. Passing `() => 0` states that input, as `civ1-science/tests/Player.action.test.ts` already does with `() => 0.5`.

Stage 3 of the engine serialisation plan, completing what `registerRules.ts` started. Events bound to the singleton `Engine` and the event factories took their registries from singleton defaults, so a second game in the same process had no handlers of its own — its turn loop would never start.

Stage 4 of the engine serialisation plan. `static transient` declares the fields a class does not want saved, `allTransient()` collects them across the inheritance chain, and `stateKeys()` reports what would be saved.

Opt-out, not opt-in: a field added later is saved by default, so forgetting to declare one wastes bytes. The reverse loses data silently, and a save format that quietly drops a new field is worse than one carrying a few it did not need.

`allTransient()` walks the prototype chain because `static` members are inherited rather than merged — a subclass declaring its own `transient` *replaces* its parent's, so without the walk `Derived` would silently start saving `_id` and `_keys` again. There is a test for exactly that.

What belongs in `transient` is anything the loading game supplies rather than the file: registries, the engine, the generator. Stage 3 is what makes that a clean idea — every constructor already takes those as parameters and a `Game` holds them, so a transient field is not a hole in the save, it is a field with a different source. Caches belong there too, for a different reason: they are derived, so restoring one restores a stale answer.
`stateKeys()` is only possible at all because of Stage 1. With `#private` fields `Object.keys` returned nothing, so no generic serialiser could exist.
